title: Japan's Disaster Day reminder: keep about one month of toilet paper, not just a few emergency rolls
summary: METI used September 1 Disaster Day to repeat a very specific household target: roughly one month of toilet paper. Rule of thumb nila is about 1 roll per person per week, so 4-person household is around 16 ordinary rolls; government disaster guidance separately recommends about 7 days of toilet supplies and rolling stock for daily essentials.
why_it_matters: Toilet paper is cheap and easy to overlook, but disasters can disrupt logistics even when factories are still producing. Having a normal rolling stock avoids panic buying and removes one basic hygiene problem during an outage or evacuation period.

claims.text: METI recommends that households keep roughly one month of toilet paper as a normal stockpile.
claims.basis: METI Disaster Day guidance published September 1, 2026

claims.text: METI's rule of thumb is about one ordinary roll per person per week; for a four-person household it gives about 16 rolls for one month.
claims.basis: METI's stated consumption and household example

claims.text: METI recommends rolling stock—using older stock first and replenishing continuously—and notes that compact long-roll products can reduce storage space.

Government disaster guidance gives a separate minimum toilet-preparedness benchmark of roughly seven days, including 5–6 portable-toilet uses per person per day and about eight 30-meter toilet-paper rolls for a four-person family.
Japan's public disaster guidance commonly calls for at least three days and preferably about one week of key household supplies such as food, water and hygiene items.
claims.basis: Cabinet Office public-opinion-survey briefing material on household stockpiles

claims.text: Keeping one month of toilet paper via rolling stock is a low-effort way to exceed the shorter emergency baseline for this specific consumable without treating it as a separate emergency-only purchase.
claims.basis: Inference from the specific toilet-paper recommendation and general emergency-stock guidance

reading_levels.30_sec: PREPARE: METI says keep about 1 month of toilet paper. Rule of thumb: 1 roll/person/week; 4 people ≈16 ordinary rolls. Use rolling stock so nothing sits forgotten. Government guidance separately says plan roughly 7 days of toilet supplies.
reading_levels.2_min: This is not a call to hoard. METI's recommendation is to maintain a normal one-month buffer and rotate through it. The logic is logistics: after a disaster or sudden demand spike, shelves can empty faster than production can replenish stores. For toilet use more broadly, government guidance suggests 5–6 portable-toilet uses per person per day for seven days plus toilet paper; its example for a family of four is about eight 30-meter rolls for seven days. The one-month METI figure is therefore a toilet-paper-specific resilience target, not a claim that every emergency item needs a month of stock.
reading_levels.deep: Do a five-minute household audit: count usable rolls, estimate household size, check whether portable toilet bags/absorbent sets exist, and place the oldest toilet-paper packs where they will be used first. Do not create a hidden 'emergency pile' that expires or gets damp. Rolling stock works because the emergency supply is also ordinary inventory.

content.who_is_affected: Households in Japan, especially families that would struggle to shop during a disaster, supply disruption or temporary isolation.
content.when: Do it now following Disaster Day, then maintain the level continuously through normal shopping.
content.financial_impact: Usually only a timing shift in normal household spending: the recommendation is to hold more of a product you already consume, not to buy a specialized high-cost kit.
content.risk_if_ignored: A disaster or short-term buying surge can leave stores temporarily short of toilet paper and other hygiene supplies, forcing emergency shopping when transport or logistics may already be impaired.
content.deadline: No hard legal deadline. Best done before the next disruption; September's Disaster Day is a practical trigger to audit stock.
content.potential_benefit: One fewer hygiene/logistics problem during an emergency, with minimal waste if the stock is rotated normally.
content.downside: Storage space. Avoid panic buying; build toward the target gradually and use long-roll/compact products if space is tight.
content.what_would_change_mind: Adjust the quantity if household consumption is materially different from METI's rule of thumb or if updated official disaster guidance changes the target.

pr_vs_reality.official_claim: METI recommends about one month of household toilet-paper stock.
evidence_says: The target is specific to toilet paper; broader government emergency-stock guidance often uses at least three days to about one week for many essentials.
Rolling stock avoids turning the recommendation into unnecessary hoarding.
pr_vs_reality.verdict: Practical and low-cost: keep a buffer, rotate it, and do not panic-buy.
